title: Red Eyes - Viral Conjunctivitis
patient_instructions: You are Chloe, a 25-year-old university student who has come to the practice with red, sore eyes. Open with: 'Doctor, my eyes have gone really red and they're a bit sore.' Story if asked: it started about three days ago in one eye and has now spread to both. There is a clear, watery discharge, and your eyelids feel a bit crusty in the morning. The soreness is a mild burning sensation, not deep pain, and does NOT get worse when you move your eyes. No itch (or only very mild). Your vision is normal - you can read fine. No double vision, no light sensitivity, no flashes or floaters. You had a runny nose and flu-like symptoms last week. Your housemate has exactly the same red-eye symptoms right now. You do NOT wear contact lenses. No fever, no headache, no nausea, no rash, no trauma, no recent overseas travel. Your idea: 'Is it pink eye? Is it contagious?' Your concern: you have exams next week and are worried about spreading it and whether you need antibiotics. Your expectation: to know what it is and what to do. Affect: mildly self-conscious about how red the eyes look, otherwise well.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. Chloe, a 25-year-old woman, presents with red and sore eyes. Take a focused history over about six minutes, then explain to the patient the most probable diagnosis and your differential diagnoses. No photograph is provided. You may state to the examiner any examination you would perform (including testing visual acuity).
examiner_instructions: The most probable diagnosis is viral conjunctivitis, supported by clear watery discharge, a preceding viral URTI, an affected housemate, normal vision and absence of red flags. Reward candidates who state they would test and record visual acuity, and who screen for the red-eye red flags that would change the diagnosis: severe ocular pain, reduced/lost vision, marked photophobia, diplopia, abnormal corneal signs, and especially contact-lens wear (never assume simple conjunctivitis in a lens wearer - exclude microbial keratitis). Do not accept laterality alone as a discriminator - conjunctivitis is usually bilateral and often starts unilateral; a persistent truly unilateral red eye should raise suspicion of keratitis, iritis or foreign body. Credit a self-limiting management plan with hygiene advice and safety-netting, and awareness that steroids must never be used if HSV is suspected. Prompt once if visual acuity is not addressed: 'Is there anything you would examine or check?'

criteria: Explores redness pattern (site, one vs both eyes, timing, progression) and characterises any pain including pain on eye movement
Clarifies discharge (colour, watery vs thick) and asks about itch, sticky lids on waking
Screens eye red-flag symptoms: vision, diplopia, photophobia, flashes/floaters
Elicits key risk/context factors: contact lenses, affected contacts (housemate), preceding URTI, trauma, travel
Reaches viral conjunctivitis with correct supporting reasoning (clear watery discharge, contact, preceding URTI, normal vision)
Differentiates viral from bacterial (thick purulent discharge) and allergic (itch, atopic background, bilateral)
Gives a structured differential and does not rely on laterality alone; keeps serious causes (keratitis, iritis, glaucoma) in mind
States would test and record visual acuity
Recognises red-eye red flags for urgent ophthalmology referral (severe pain, visual loss, photophobia, diplopia, contact-lens wearer)
Gives self-limiting supportive plan (cool compresses, lubricants, strict hand hygiene, do not share towels) with safety-netting; avoids steroids where HSV possible
Explains diagnosis, contagiousness and hygiene measures in plain language and checks understanding
Addresses patient's concerns (exams, antibiotics, spread) and safety-nets clearly

red_flags: Severe ocular pain or reduced/lost vision - urgent ophthalmology referral (not simple conjunctivitis)
Contact-lens wearer with a red painful eye - exclude microbial (bacterial/acanthamoeba) keratitis; never assume conjunctivitis
Marked photophobia, diplopia, dilated/irregular pupil or abnormal corneal signs - consider keratitis, iritis/uveitis or acute glaucoma
Persistent truly unilateral red eye - beware keratitis, iritis or foreign body
Suspected herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic ulcer, prior cold sores) - never use topical steroids
australian_guidelines: Murtagh red-eye golden rules - always test and record vision; beware the unilateral red eye; conjunctivitis is almost always bilateral; never use steroids if herpes simplex is suspected
Murtagh red-eye red flags for urgent ophthalmic referral - severe ocular pain, loss of vision, diplopia, abnormal corneal signs, microbial keratitis with contact-lens use
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - viral conjunctivitis is self-limiting; supportive care and strict hygiene; antibiotics not indicated for viral conjunctivitis
RACGP / infection control - hand hygiene, avoid sharing towels/linen, and work/study exclusion advice to limit spread of contagious conjunctivitis
learning_objectives: Take a structured red-eye history and reach a probable diagnosis of viral conjunctivitis
Differentiate viral, bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis using discharge, itch and atopic background
Apply the red-eye golden rules, including always testing visual acuity and being wary of the unilateral red eye
Recognise red-eye red flags and the special risk of a contact-lens wearer with a painful red eye
key_points: Conjunctivitis is almost always bilateral and often starts in one eye then spreads; laterality alone is not a reliable discriminator.
Viral discharge is clear and watery; bacterial discharge is thick and purulent; allergic conjunctivitis is itch-dominant on an atopic background.
Always test and record visual acuity - reduced vision, severe pain or photophobia point away from simple conjunctivitis.
Never assume simple conjunctivitis in a contact-lens wearer, and never use steroids if HSV keratitis is possible.

citations.claim: The painful red eye has a defined red-flag differential (keratitis, uveitis/iritis, episcleritis, scleritis, acute glaucoma, corneal ulcer, endophthalmitis) and urgent-referral red flags including severe ocular pain, loss of vision, diplopia and microbial keratitis with contact-lens use.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1175

citations.claim: Red-eye golden rules: always test and record vision, beware of the unilateral red eye, and conjunctivitis is almost always bilateral - correcting the claim that infective conjunctivitis is usually unilateral.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1207

citations.claim: Herpes simplex is characterised by recurrent painful lesions - relevant to the red-eye rule that steroids must never be used if HSV keratitis is suspected.
